Mr. Speaker, with the recent announcement of the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Fraser) that the fishing vessel insurance plan will be phased out between now and 1986, fishermen in my community, and indeed in all of Canada, will be devastated by this move.
The original reason for government intervention in the vessel insurance business was because the private sector was not meeting the needs of fishermen. Fishermen will now have to deal with private companies to insure their boats. subsubtopic: IMPORTANCE OF INDUSTRY TO BRITISH COLUMBIA- GOVERNMENT COMMITMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, forestry is Canada's most important renewable resource. Nearly one million people are directly or indirectly dependent upon the forestry industry for employment. In British Columbia, one out of every four people rely on this vital industry.
Yesterday in the House the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) reiterated his real commitment to this important national industry. He told the House that a healthy forest industry is vital to our national economic renewal. More important, the Prime Minister assured British Columbians, and all Canadians, that the Government intends to bring substantial help to the forest industry in British Columbia.
For the first time in two decades the federal Government has brought forestry to the top of the list of economic priorities. A new era of federal-provincial co-operation has dawned, and new forestry agreements are being negotiated. The Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) and the Prime Minister will ensure that Canada's once vibrant forest industry is revitalized. We British Columbians welcome this new attitude and this new commitment.

subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF WOMEN AGED 50 TO 65 YEARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Progressive Conservative Government has asked Hon. Members and the people of Canada to present alternatives designed to make our social programs more effective. At the present time a percentage of public money goes into the pockets of the wealthy. Even though some of it is taxed back, it is my personal view that there are ways to make our programs more effective.
The biggest gap in social programs today affects women between the ages of 50 and 65 who are in dire need and receive nothing except welfare. This group includes single women who spent their working years looking after aged parents or a crippled or a mentally retarded brother or sister. Divorcees, or women whose husbands died young, and those who scrubbed floors to keep their families together, never had the opportunity to pay into the Canada Pension Plan, and now they are unable to find work even if their health permits it.
I ask the Liberals and members of the NDP who are so insistent upon nothing being taken away from the wealthy: What do you tell these women who are existing on meagre welfare while the rich simply deposit the public money and thus become richer?
I commend the Government for looking into social programs. I present the needy women between the ages of 50 and 65 as a priority group who need help. Only the very greedy will criticize a social program which effectively helps the people who need help the most.

That this House recognizes the extreme urgency of the unemployment crisis in Atlantic Canada, and urges the government to move immediately on a major program of regional development based on:
1.	proper resource management to rebuild the forestry, fishing and coal industries;
2.	self-directed community programs to expand permanent jobs through co-coperatives and small business;
3.	affirmative action to remove job barriers faced by women; and
4.	government led investment to expand and safeguard jobs in the steel industry through Devco (Cape Breton Development Corporation).
He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to speak to you and to this House of Commons today with an extreme sense of urgency about the difficulties and dangers that face our country, as we have heard this past week, throughout Atlantic Canada. There has to be action now on the many problems of unemployment that have built up over the years and have reached a state of extreme urgency in this past period of increasingly heavy unemployment there.
I want to tell the Members of the House of Commons what groups like the St. Joseph's Parish unemployed group of Sydney told us. Young people are desperate for jobs-jobs for the long run, not the kind of short-run, make-work jobs which have too often characterized what has been taking place in Atlantic Canada. That group requested a Canada Works grant and was turned down. They report that in Cape Breton over 40

January 25, 1985
Supply
per cent of the potential workforce is out of work. In a town like Glace Bay, over 60 per cent is out of work.
I want to report what groups like the YMCA job corps in Newfoundland said to our action group, that the real unemployment rate in the Province of Newfoundland is between 39 and 45 per cent. Over 50 per cent of high school students are dropping out and finding themselves without a future in the workforce of that province. There is a despair that results for the people of that province, particularly the young people.
I want to report what we heard from the vice-president of the Newcastle-Chatham District Labour Council. Over 18,000 employable people exist in Miramichi, New Brunswick, 8,000 of whom are on UIC and 2,000 on social assistance. Over 50 per cent of the workforce in that part of New Brunswick is unemployed.

This young student at the University of Moncton told us: "It may be the International Year of Youth, but as far as the young people in Moncton are concerned, it must be International Unemployment Year".

I have to report what we heard from the Status of Women group in St. John's, Newfoundland. Over 45 per cent of women in that province are jobless. Those women face serious job barriers. For them it is a depression, not a recession. For them the time for polite words is past.
The problem is immense. Official statistics show that unemployment, despite some decrease nationally, is up significantly in Atlantic Canada. In Newfoundland it is up on seasonally adjusted rates from 19 per cent a year ago to over 21 per cent. In Prince Edward Island it is up two percentage points to 13.5 per cent from a year ago. In Nova Scotia it is not up quite as much but it is up. New Brunswick is virtually the same. The participation rates for the population throughout Atlantic Canada are significantly lower in the workforce than in the rest of this country. The rate in Canada for participation in the workforce is 65 per cent, but in Newfoundland it is only 53.5 per cent, 61 per cent in Nova Scotia and 55.7 per cent in New Brunswick.
These figures tell us that there are people who, if they lived in the rest of Canada, would be in the workforce but because they live in Atlantic Canada cannot find jobs. That is why the real rate of unemployment reported to us by people is actually 30 per cent to 45 per cent in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
It is a chronic problem. As the social justice network in Cape Breton Island told us, it is a problem that has existed for many years but is far, far worse as we begin 1985. As the Nova Scotia Federation of Labour said to us, if we had this level of unemployment throughout the entire country, there would be a revolution here. We must do something about this problem and we must move fast because its social effects are catastrophic.
Professors from the university in Moncton spoke to us about increased violence and suicides in New Brunswick. The health coalition in Cape Breton Island told us that referrals to hospitals for mental health problems have gone up by over 50 per cent in the last seven years.
Now there are new fears that people in Atlantic Canada feel as they look at the first steps taken by the new Government to try to deal with the regional development problems in that part of Canada. There is a sense of fear and concern that has been created by the cuts that have taken place and also, frankly, by some problems in the consultation process as it begins. I would like to relate publicly what I heard from people in Atlantic Canada. Some Ministers have made good starts on consultation but there have been some serious problems with other Ministers and a sense of unease hangs over the region. For instance, we heard from the New Brunswick Federation of Woodlot Owners, a group of small business people and farmers who produce almost 30 per cent of the wood output of the province yet have received only 16 per cent of the reforestation funding available through the federal-provincial agreement. We were told that that group met on December 15 with the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) who, after all, comes from New Brunswick. Yet in six weeks there has been no response from the Minister to the request that the formula dividing those funds for reforestation efforts be changed to give them a fair share. The group has asked for more fairness because that fairness could give an estimated 350 more jobs per year in New Brunswick. Yet no answer has been given by the Government.
The Cape Breton Council of Senior Citizens told us about its serious concerns regarding what will happen to people facing the possibility of early retirement in industry in order to open up jobs for young people. The UIC cuts proposed by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) will have the effect of eliminating the possibility of receiving UIC during the first early retirement year as of the end of this year. Older people in Cape Breton Island are scared.
[ Translation]
Students and professors at the University of Moncton talked about the CBC cutbacks in Moncton, but there have also been cuts in Gander and Cape Breton. The problems created by these cutbacks for the Francophone community of New Brunswick are very considerable.

Those kinds of cuts are scaring people in Atlantic Canada because they see their ability to speak for themselves through these important national media being cut away.
The Maritime Fishermen's Union, for example, told us they entered with a sense of responsibility and hope into negotiations about the division of fish quotas in the Cape Breton area between inshore fishermen and large-scale fishermen. They compromised and worked out an agreement. They felt that they had come to an agreement that was not perfect or exactly what they wanted.
January 25, 1985

However, they had reached an agreement which they felt they could live with. Yet the Minister, in the final agreement which was established, moved it in almost the opposite direction from the direction that had been negotiated. There is a sense of profound unease felt by those fishermen about the real meaning of consultation.
We heard about the fears of the people of Glace Bay who face a cut in the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program to 25 per cent of last year's allocation. That program is an important source of jobs in that community. We heard from the United Mine Workers and the Nova Scotia Federation of Labour about their concern over the remarks made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) who spoke about perhaps getting rid of Devco and privatizing the coal mines in Cape Breton Island. That suggestion may go down very well with her constituents in British Columbia but it scares people and communities in Altantic Canada.
As our action group spoke to 45 or 50 groups in the days we were there, we sensed a growing lack of confidence and a search for alternatives to the direction in which the Government seems to be heading. However, it is important to stress that we also sensed a feeling of hope and potential for communities in Atlantic Canada. Despite the problems that exist and despite how urgently action is needed, Atlantic Canada is not a basket case. People in that part of the country are tired of condescension from central Canada. They are tired of control by central Canada, whether it be control by large companies like Noranda in New Brunswick or Abitibi-Price in Newfoundland or control by bureaucrats from central Canada. They are tired of control by bureaucrats from an organization like Devco which, despite much of its contribution, has created a sense among the United Mine Workers and the steelworkers in Cape Breton that it is not prepared to consult honestly, openly and completely with the workers who will be so profoundly affected by Devco's decisions.
These people, Mr. Speaker, have given us some exciting ideas about the future. The motion which we have put before the House today tries to summarize, not in detail but with some particulars, the kinds of hopes which we heard and which we felt. There was hope first for resource development which will operate through small groups and organizations instead of just the large companies. For instance, Mr. Speaker, we were told that reforestation efforts in Newfoundland could give us a thousand extra jobs a year if this Government and the Government of that province would get together and move fast on just those kinds of initiatives. I have already mentioned the 350 jobs which the woodlot owners in New Brunswick are convinced could come from their being given more responsibility for reforestation.
The same thing is true in the fishing industry. The Newfoundland fishermen's union told us very clearly of its plans and hopes to build that industry in Newfoundland through community-owned fishing plants which would not have to rely
Supply
on the large external companies which do not have the sensitivity of or roots in local communities.
I have to mention coal as well, Mr. Speaker. The United Mine Workers Union has come up with what I consider an imaginative, exciting plan for re-establishing and refurbishing the coal industry in Cape Breton. I am very pleased that the Minister who is responsible in this area has encouraged this plan. However, this hope must not be allowed to become a forlorn hope. It must be something which the Government comes through on and we, Mr. Speaker, will be pushing to see that that does happen.
It is not just resources. The resource base of Atlantic Canada is important to build on but we have to go beyond that. We must use the human resource in Atlantic Canada because that human resource is there. There is a sense all across the communities which we visited that people themselves, working together, acting in a self-reliant way, can build future jobs for themselves. They can work it through, as is happening in Glace Bay, small businesses set up in an incubator mall there which is going to provide a great many jobs. It is exactly the same kind of thing with co-operatives. However, as these jobs expand, as group after group told us, there must also be fairness for women. In the basic industries of that region as well there must be an emphasis on growth in shipbuilding and in steel.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, I would say that if this happens, if this hope is realized, we can turn around the extremely serious problems of that part of Canada and deal with the most urgent concern of unemployment which is so badly hitting the people of those communities.

speechtext: Questions or comments? There being no questions or comments, I call on the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens).

speakeroldname: Hon. Sinclair Stevens (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) for his motion. I say that because it gives me an opportunity to bring the House up to date on many of the initiatives which this Government has taken in regional development and small business encouragement over the past few months and, in particular, over the past few weeks. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, last evening when I first saw the motion I was so pleased with its contents, the setting out of the four points, that for a moment I thought it had probably been proposed by, say, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton Highlands-Canso (Mr. O'Neil) or the Hon. Member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain), both of whom, I think Hon. Members would agree, are very able advocates in the Government caucus of development at a regional level, especially in Atlantic Canada. However, upon checking I found that indeed the motion had been brought forward by our socialist friend who, after presenting the motion today and giving us an opportunity to hear his remarks, seems to have fallen into that pitfall which the socialists continually fall into, and that is their plaintive voice of despair. We have nothing to fear in this country and despair will only bring more despair.

January 25, 1985
Supply
As you are no doubt aware, Mr. Speaker, earlier this week, on Monday in fact, I met with my counterparts, the Ministers responsible for regional development at the provincial level and in the two territories, and I only wish that Hon. Members who are going to participate in this debate could have sat in and listened to the positive, co-operative and optimistic spirit which prevailed at that meeting with every provincial representative and every representative of the territories. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I have had literally a majority of those who attended either write to me or speak to me, saying that it has been the best meeting of a regional development nature that they have ever attended, certainly the best that they have attended in the last three and a half years. I say that because I believe we should bear in mind that the agenda which was worked out at that meeting was one which we now intend to put to the First Ministers' conference in Regina. We are hoping that many of the things which were agreed to at our meeting on Monday will be furthered and recommended by the First Ministers in Regina.
I can tell you that Atlantic Canada will be very pleased if some of the things which have been agreed to at our level are also agreed to at that First Ministers' conference. Having said that, I would like to remind Hon. Members that on the government side there are Ministers and Hon. Members who are determined to harness a team to take up the challenges of regional economic development, taking it out of whatever is its low point and turning it into a successful, dynamic development in the regions which need it most in this country.
What we are hearing from the opposition side are the cynical platitudes of those who only know how to ride this question as a hobby horse. The provincial Ministers with whom I have met know the difference. They are prepared to be part of our team approach. The provincial First Ministers will meet with our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) next month in Regina, as I have indicated, and they hopefully will also set the guidelines and directions for the team approach we are hoping to accomplish. We would welcome constructive ideas, of course, from all sides so I invite those on hobby horses to get down and join the real team which will do a real job for all parts of Canada.
As the House is aware, regional development is one of the four major topics with which those First Ministers in Regina will be dealing. It was put on the Regina agenda at Meech Lake. Of course, I cannot in good faith reveal the details of the discussions I have referred to that were conducted on Monday, but I can say that we had cordial and frank discussions and we have broken new ground in our deliberations.
In view of the lip service paid by the former Government to regional development, I am sure the House will be as surprised as I was to learn that the meeting last Monday was the first time there has been such a meeting of regional development Ministers in Canada throughout our entire history. Such a meeting has never been held before in our Confederation. I feel that coming out of this meeting there has been a new sense
of direction established. There has been a reconfirmation that the day of unilateral federal regional development is over. In fact, there was a new commitment to the principle that we work together, we consult and, wherever possible, we co-ordinate our activities.
Coming out of this we agreed that there will be additional meetings soon. The actual timing of these meetings and their place we would hope would be one of the items again to be dealt with by the First Ministers in Regina.
Turning now to the specifics of regional development in Atlantic Canada, I suggest that our Prime Minister summed it up in Halifax last August when he stated, and let me quote his words:
All of Canada has been the victim of 20 years of failed Liberal policies, but this failure has been most evident in Atlantic Canada. It is here where the Liberal legacy is most apparent, it is here where failed Liberal policies and broken promises have had their most damaging effects.
As the Minister now responsible for implementing many of the programs we put in place to address the problems of regional development, I realize that this failure was not as much a failure of the programs themselves as a failure to co-operate and co-ordinate programs with provincial initiatives and aims. As background to our deliberations and to set regional development in the Atlantic Provinces in a proper perspective, I would like to point out that major federal economic development commitments in the Atlantic provinces, including signed agreements with the provinces, total at the present time some $5 billion. To say the least, that is a handsome figure in any person's calculation. While many of these commitments extend into the 1990s, such as the Atlantic fisheries restructuring and the Atlantic region's share of the patrol frigate program, a large portion of these funds will be spent during the life of the Parliament we are now sitting in.
Let me now turn to the specifics raised and to point one in the resolution before us. It deals with the proper resource management to rebuild the forestry, fishing and coal industries in the Atlantic provinces. I hope Hon. Members are aware that this Department has now committed $23.5 million to the Maritime Forest Research Centre in New Brunswick, some $475 million to the Atlantic fisheries, and $493 million to the coal industry. In addition, under the economic and regional development agreements, the Government of Canada has committed $4 million to the pulp and paper industry in Newfoundland, $12.5 million to forestry resource development in Prince Edward Island, $12 million in Nova Scotia and $42.3 million in New Brunswick. As well as carrying out the Atlantic fisheries restructuring program and commitments resulting from the Kirby report, Fisheries and Oceans has committed an additional $67.5 million to Fisheries Departments in the Atlantic region.
While the legislation governing the economic and regional development agreements calls for consultation and subsequent adjustments as necessary on the anniversary date of signing, two Atlantic provinces, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, have indicated they want earlier meetings. I can assure Hon. Members we intend to meet that request by those two
January 25, 1985

provinces. These anniversary meetings provide an excellent opportunity to review the work accomplished over the past year under the agreement, to make any necessary corrections, to develop new development thrusts as dictated by experience, and to meet the ever-changing conditions in the most effective manner. I am certain that these meetings will be held in the same atmosphere of mutual respect and co-operation that was so evident at our meeting on Monday.
Let me deal with the second point raised by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor. This Government has from the beginning made it clear that the road to prosperity in Canada rested on the private sector and, in particular, small business in Canada. Now, his motion refers to the self-directed community programs to expand permanent jobs through co-operative and small businesses. This Government has promised that it would create an atmosphere of confidence in the private sector so that it might carry out its task of getting Canadians back into the workforce. This, then, has been our major thrust in the small business sector. This does not mean that the federal Government is going to shirk its responsibilities in the field of regional development but, rather, that it will accomplish the over-all objectives of maximizing regional development through co-operation rather than confrontation.
That this policy is working out was emphasized this week by the release of a Conference Board of Canada survey which showed that Canadian companies planned to do more research and development in coming years. In its survey of 200 companies it found that these Canadian firms plan to increase R and D spending by about 7 per cent per year from now through until 1989. That level is well above the expected rate of inflation over those years and is a strong indication that business has decided to go for real-growth in home grown R and D. I would suggest that this is but one indication, and there are many others I could cite, that the private sector is indeed willing to do its share with new-found and well-founded confidence.
In coming months, very soon in fact, we will be making announcements concerning new activities, new things starting in Atlantic Canada, that I know all of those who get off that hobbyhorse of wanting to play it as a political dodge will welcome.
Since coming into office the Department has made changes to the Industrial and Regional Development Program which will have a profound effect on the processing of small business grant applications. As Members know in particular, the institution of automatic maximum sharing ratios for projects requiring less than $100,000 in Crown support ensures that this smaller type of assistance may be processed speedily, with certainty, and at the local level. That is exactly what we understand is wanted from the small business sector.
In a similar vein, the changes in the Investment Canada Bill tabled in this House and now in second reading will remove many of the aggravations inherent in the Foreign Investment Review Act. In particular, the raising of the threshold for consideration in effect removes most small businesses from the former long and sometimes tedious approval process. I find it
Supply
startling, though, that when you are trying to do something as positive as we are trying to do with Investment Canada, something which is going to have a profound effect in starting new businesses in Atlantic Canada, it is the self same socialists and their allies, the official Liberal opposition, that are now blocking that legislation and denying future jobs for Canadians through their blockade in this House.
Hear, hear!

Another indication of our support for the small business sector came this week when I tabled amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act which raise the loan ceiling in the aggregate by $300 million and raise the gross revenue of those businesses entitled to apply from $1.5 million to $2 million. We will have further announcements in this sector when the present consultative process with the small business community is completed.
Our Department has taken the affirmative action program initiated by Treasury Board for government employees and also encourages firms bidding on projects supported by the federal Government to adopt affirmative action programs. As a matter of record, we have just completed a study of our Department's hiring practices in order to assess any problems that may exist and remove any barriers that exist. This study will be forwarded to Treasury Board in the next few days. Affirmative action is a commitment of our Prime Minister which we are implementing with as much speed and fairness as is humanly possible.
With all due respect to the Hon. Member, I think he is perhaps a little confused when he refers to steel and Devco. Of course, as Hon. Members who are well acquainted with this area know, Devco is not in the steel business, it is in the coal business.
Over the years I think we should not forget that the federal Government has made an enormous financial commitment to Cape Breton through Devco. In the past five years it has provided over $.5 billion in direct funding. This year alone the Government will spend about $150 million on Devco which in turn employs some 3,400 people on the island. In support of our commitment to Cape Breton and Devco last year I made a tour of the island which included some of the mining projects and facilities to familiarize myself with the situation. I can assure Hon. Members that the Government is committed to strengthening the operations of Devco to ensure that the coal industry will continue to play an important economic role in the future of the Atlantic region. Positive announcements will be coming very soon with respect to that company.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like once again to thank the Member for Essex-Windsor for affording me this opportunity briefly to review the present Government's continuing commitment to regional development in Atlantic Canada. This commitment was appropriately summed up by our Prime Minister last year when he said:

We recognize that the kind of assistance that will be required to prepare for the economic opportunities of the 1980s and 1990s is not within the financial resources of the provincial and local Governments in the region, and that the federal Government has a responsibility, within the limit of its own resources, to fill that gap. We recognize too that the only way to ensure that appropriate policies are identified and tailored to match changing realities is to involve the people of Atlantic Canada as much as possible in planning the economic development of their own communities.
I will assure Hon. Members that this week's meeting of Ministers responsible for regional development throughout Canada is an important step in this process, not only for Atlantic Canada but for regional development in every region and area of this great country of ours that will once again boom under a new private enterprise-oriented Government.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have a short question for the Minister. He referred with a great deal of fierte or pride to the fact that the Government is moving very quickly on affirmative action. Can he tell the House today in a very definitive and precise way what the timetable is now for the Abella report? In Atlantic Canada we ran across many problems with women, young people and the disabled. They are very concerned about the Government's timetable for the Abella report which speaks very strongly about employment equity and affirmative action in the country. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald) has said that they are studying it and moving quickly. What is the timetable?

Mr. Speaker, one of the nice things about the Hon. Member is that often in asking a question he also answers it. He has referred to the Minister of Employment and Immigration who is responsible with respect to the Abella report. I suggest that the Hon. Member direct the question to that Minister.
Mr. Speaker, is the Minister saying that he does not know what is going on?
Mr. Speaker, I can reassure the Hon. Member that we as a Cabinet work together. We allow all of our Ministers to speak for themselves, and in no way do I intend to alter that course.

Mr. Speaker, as the Minister very well knows, regional development has linkages with other government departments. We have heard negative speculation that the nautical institute which has been earmarked for Port Hawkesbury, Nova Scotia, in the seat of my colleague from Cape Breton Highlands-Canso will not be honoured, but that that amount of money will be expended in the City of Halifax.

Mr. Speaker, I am not in a position to make any comment on what the Hon. Member has referred to. I would remind him that as chairman of the Cabinet committee for economic and regional development I am in the happy position of being able to co-ordinate all of the various departments and Ministers that he refers to. I can assure him that a very high priority of that co-ordination is to ensure that there will be effective and early regional economic development.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy that the Minister has acknowledged that there are linkages between various departments of government. I am happy that he is the chairman of the Cabinet committee. Would the Minister not think it only fair and appropriate, in view of the devastating economy in Atlantic Canada, that they review their expenditures within the envelope of housing so that RRAP, as we refer to it, could revert back to the expenditures of previous years? As the Minister knows, expenditures in that regard have a very good effect in the sense that the economic multiplier is greatest in the housing industry. Could he comment on that?

Mr. Speaker, I know that the Hon. Member is perhaps relatively new to the House, but I hope he would not fall into the tremendous trap that so many of his colleagues who are so chained to the past have fallen into. They can only think in terms of spending programs and governmental intervention and interference. We are into a new era. Come up and enjoy it in the 1980s and I think you will see prosperity, better housing and better accommodation. A better living standard for people will once again start to be the rule rather than the exception in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it has become clear that at least one resource that the Minister is committed to increasing with respect to Atlantic Canada is red herrings. A tremendous number of interesting points have been made to us that have very little to do with questions of regional development in Atlantic Canada. I am very pleased to hear about affirmative action programs in his own ministry, but I suggest, with respect, that there is a great deal more in direct terms which needs to be done for Atlantic Canada.
I have some specific questions for the Minister which deal with points that were raised with us during our action group's visit. If he is unable to answer these questions himself, perhaps he can get his colleagues to answer the people of Atlantic Canada.
First, will the Minister see to it that the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) gives a reply to the New Brunswick Federation of Woodlot Owners with respect to their request for a change in the sharing of facilities for reforestation under that federal-provincial agreement?
Second, will the Minister use the auspices of Devco or Sysco? As the Minister knows, Devco does coal industrial development as well as coal mining in Cape Breton.
Will he use those mechanisms to see to it that the United Steel Workers in Cape Breton get a response to their request about the second phase of the expansion of Sysco?
Third, will the Minister see to it that the status of women group in Newfoundland gets a response to its request that Canada Works programs be equitably shared between men and women in Newfoundland?
Fourth, will the Minister see to it that his Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) at least meets with those who
January 25, 1985

are concerned with the cut-backs of the Cape Breton CBC service? A committee has been trying for months to get such a meeting.
Fifth, will the Minister finally respond to the concerns about which many in Atlantic Canada have asked concerning the UIC cuts which hit not just those facing early retirement options but a great many people who are worried about the possibility of tighter regulations in the future?
Can the Minister respond to those kinds of specifics on behalf of his Government?

Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member is aware, having thrown about five questions at me, it is absolutely impossible within our rules for me to respond fully to those five or six questions. I can assure the Hon. Member that if he would like to write to me and ask those questions, or if he wants to take it now as notice to me, he will get a full reply to all of his questions.
Why didn't you do it in the speech?
He didn't ask them.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) went to New York and spoke to the Economic Club. He essentially said: "Come and buy out anything you want in Canada". Since we have this policy of no questions asked regardless of how many manufacturing concerns are going to be shut down or whatever, and since we are debating Atlantic Canada, I would be interested to know, as a result of this request by the Prime Minister and the glowing position that the Minister has indicated with his Investment Canada Bill, which some people have graciously called a "sell out Canada Bill", exactly how many additional applications he has received under the present FIRA legislation as a result of this new policy which the Minister says will bring thousands of new businesses to Canada?
I would be interested to know what the dollar value has been for Atlantic Canada. In addition, I would like to hear how many new applications there have been and what the increase in applications has been under present FIRA rules for new industries coming into Atlantic Canada.

The Foreign Investment Review Act is still the law of the land. We would like to change it. There is no new law. We have to implement the same provisions that have been in place for the last ten years. When the Member asks is there a great flood or are there new applicants, I have to tell him that there is no change in the law. We are suggesting that there should be a change, that there should be a more positive approach. I would like the

Hon. Member's support to put that more positive approach in place so we can allow these applications to start flooding in.
I can also assure you, Mr. Speaker, that even in anticipation of there being a healthier and more welcome climate in this country for foreign investment, we have had literally dozens of inquiries as to when the new act will be in place so people can be received in a more wholesome way.
If the Hon. Member is wanting any independent evidence as to how on a world-wide basis this country has made foreign capital unwelcome, I ask him to read the European Management Forum which now reports that out of 28 countries reviewed, Canada stands twenty-eighth in our hostility to foreign investment. Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), for putting forward this motion today and for reporting back to the House on some of his travels in Atlantic Canada with regard to the problems with which people in that area are confronted.
I want to tell him, and particularly the Minister responsible for Regional Industrial Development (Mr. Stevens), that I believe the solutions to these problems are political ones. I believe the solutions rest with the Minister leading the way and seeking the co-operation of the private sector.
I would like very briefly before I have to terminate my remarks at one o'clock to read to the Minister a sentence of a report which was submitted to the Royal Commission on Economic Union and Development Prospects for Canada. According to the Pictou County Research and Development Commission dated October 12, 1983, any new solutions to the unemployment problem must put jobs and incomes for disadvantaged communities at the beginning of the list of priorities. Without this strategy, existing disadvantaged communities will continue to be the victims of progress.
When you look at what this Conservative Government has done, Mr. Speaker, since taking office, you will see emphasis has been put on the words jobs, jobs for Canadians.
It is jobs, jobs, jobs. Three jobs.

With this statement here, the Tories are certainly not following their own rhetoric or the rhetoric of others.
I would like to point out to the Minister, who is rarely in attendance but is here today-

speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to continue with my remarks. Approximately $2.2 billion was cut from federal Government's budgetary expenditures. This means that spending originally aimed at economic and regional development represents 80 per cent of the total federal budgetary cuts.
Atlantic Canada is a region which has traditionally relied upon and benefited from federal expenditures aimed at reducing regional disparities. Our future growth and survival are vitally linked with the federal regional development policy. It is evident that the Atlantic provinces have been designated as a low priority area by the Progressive Conservative Government, as is set out in this preview to their economic master plan.
Of the $625 million dropped in loans and investments to Crown corporations, a planned equity injection of $275 million to Petro-Canada has been cancelled. Being the leading exploration force in offshore development in the Atlantic region, this reduction in the spending power of Petro-Canada can only have ill effects on the economy of the region, particularly in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland.
We in the Atlantic provinces depend heavily upon resource-based industry with the support of regional economic policy and job-creation programs initiated and assisted by the Government of Canada. Four federal departments are particularly relevant and co-related to the economy of Atlantic Canada. These are the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans and the Department of Employment and Immigration. Of the 21 departments affected by recent cuts, Energy, Mines and Resources received the highest cuts by far at $613 million; followed by Employment and Immigration at $432 million. The Department of Regional Industrial Expansion is fifth in line with $200 million slashed from its Industrial Incentives Program. Finally, a Department with a relatively small budget but one that is crucial to the development of Atlantic Canada is Fisheries and Oceans. It stands thirteenth on the list at $36.1 million, far exceeding the budgets of Justice and National Health and Welfare.
The cuts affect us in the forestry. Research cuts in forestry amount to $1.4 million. Research cuts in Fisheries and Oceans amount to another $1.5 million, In programs which assist the development of the fishing industry, the marketing of products and the development of the marine resources, again we see another cut of $11.7 million. There are cuts in ferry services, including a summer only service on the Yarmouth-Bar Harbour ferry, of $16 million. The CN budget reduction is $21 million. The Trans-Quebec and Maritime Gas Pipeline is now deferred, $8 million cut from that. Corner Brook, Newfoundland as the new location for the forest research centre has been deferred, another $3.5 million cut for Atlantic Canada. Capital expenditures for the fishing industry to manage fish stocks for hydrographic and oceanographic activities now eliminated, $18.1 million. The transfer of the Nova Scotia regional office for income security programs from Halifax to Sydney another cut of $2.1 million. Construction of a new office complex in Halifax, another cut of $14 million. Increases in berthage fees, port inspections and foreign licence fees, another $6.3 million effect on Atlantic Canada. It is clear that what we were told before the election about jobs, jobs, jobs has not materialized, notwithstanding the rhetoric of the Minister responsible nor the Government as a body.
We have seen massive cuts which have greatly affected the lives of Canadians in Atlantic Canada. I have some suggestions, continuing along the line of my friend from Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), for the Government. It is all well and good
January 25, 1985

to talk of the private sector. We in this Party support the private sector. However, to suggest as the Conservative Party has done repeatedly, particularly today, that the private sector will pick up all of the slack to create the jobs and the wealth needed in Atlantic Canada is being less than honest. The brutal fact is that there is a need for government intervention in the economy so that the less fortunate areas of this country have the opportunity to make a meaningful contribution to the Canadian economy.
What better vehicle is there than the national Government taking its role seriously and honestly? The Constitution, the accord which was signed by the provinces, states very clearly that the Government of Canada will provide assistance to the disadvantaged areas of this country, but this Government is not doing that. It is doing the exact opposite. Forestry is down from a high of 70,000 jobs in August to 9,000 in December. If that is performance in Atlantic Canada, I would hate to see anything else interpreted in that way. Fishing employment in Atlantic Canada is down from 29,000 in July to 18,000 in December. The food and beverage industry has gone from a high of 54,000 to 31,000 in December.
What about the construction industry, which affects a great host of people in Atlantic Canada? Employment is down from 29,000 to 18,000 in December. The federal administration, which comes under the direct jurisdiction of the Government of Canada, is down from 40,000 to 33,000. This Government is not taking regional development seriously. If it were, it would not be zeroing in on the less fortunate areas of this country and making its most devastating and crucial cuts on the people in that area.
It has been echoed in places other than this Chamber what the Government of Canada ought to do. Members of Parliament are aware of the difficult plight of individuals in Cape Breton and what they are faced with at the present time. I suggested to the Minister that in the interim a special agreement be developed with the Province of Nova Scotia. They ought to live up to their responsibilities to provide the infrastructure. Whether the jurisdiction is federal or provincial, it ought to be a co-operative effort. A special subsidiary agreement between the Government of Canada and the Government of Nova Scotia is crucial.
With regard to the coal industry, an answer in terms of short-term economics, and more importantly in the long-term interests of Atlantic Canada and in encouraging the Canadian economy, is a pre-retirement plan. That has been suggested time and time again, whether it be in economic reports put out by various public bodies across this country, or by provincial Governments or the federal Government.
The provisions of the ILAP program ought to be increased. Other areas in this country ought to be designated. In particular, I cite the members of the United Mine Workers of America who have been pushing this Government for a preretirement plan in order to allow older workers to retire and to provide jobs for younger workers who succeed them.
With regard to the coal industry, the people of that area are awaiting the Minister's answer with regard to his commit-
Supply
ments for a long-term project in the Town of Glace Bay. We have waited patiently. I listened to what the Minister said here earlier today. I hope he will live up to that and make an announcement forthwith, not four or six months down the road but within the next number of days. This project is absolutely essential.
The motion we are debating this afternoon calls for an injection of funds by the Government of Canada with a second phase toward the modernization of Sydney Steel. The Government has been sitting on this. That plan was not put forward by a Liberal Government but by a Tory provincial Government in the Province of Nova Scotia. It is high time that the Minister responsible and the Government of Canada lived up to the commitments of the previous Government and honoured the commitment of providing moneys for the second phase.
The forest industry is another important element of Atlantic Canada. There are approximately 148 sawmills in Atlantic Canada. Each in its own way affects various small communities. What, if anything, has this Government done to try and assist? I urge it to take its responsibility seriously. The Government ought to provide a safety net to protect laid off employees and to reduce fear of buying or constructing a home. Federal incentives for new home purchase should be a permanently instituted policy which would float as the market cycles prescribe. I urge the removal of the 5 per cent federal sales tax on lumber. Subsidies presently extended under the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the Atlantic Freight Rates Assistance Act should be increased in order to reduce the market proximity problems confronting the maritime lumber industry.
A saw mill training institute should be established in Atlantic Canada to increase productivity, reduce training and apprenticeship costs, fill the need for skilled workers capable of operating new and highly sophisticated machinery and, most importantly, to fill the shoes of an alarmingly aging workforce.
I know my time is running close. In the fishing industry, the Government ought to inject some dollars, improving marketing and promotion through research. We know what the blue book as tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has done. This Government echoes sentiments about research, but what has it done? It has cut $1.5 million from the Fisheries and Oceans research budget, that is what it has done. It has to improve, through co-operative effort with the provinces and the international community, whether the agency be called Investment Canada, our international trade or external relations, in the export of fishery products. That is a serious undertaking that the Government ought to get on with forthwith.
There are many other matters that I could touch on, but I will conclude with this because it concerns my constituency. It has to do with an economic policy built on fact, not on hypothesis or words adopted from philosophy obtained south of the border. It is all well and good to talk of the private sector. I suggest to you seriously, Sir, that the private sector does not operate in those areas of Canada with high unemploy-

January 25, 1985
Supply
ment. It may operate in terms of small business and I think we ought to do everything we can to encourage small business. However, the reality is that the private sector in Atlantic Canada cannot pick up all the slack and create the thousands of new jobs which are needed there.
The Government of Canada has a responsibility under the Canadian Constitution to provide services to all areas of the country and to provide equal opportunities for Canadians wherever they live, whether it be in Manitoba, Quebec or indeed in the Atlantic area. I note that the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) is laughing. I think it is very unfair that in a city like Halifax with some of the highest rents in the country there are slum landlords charging people as much as possible and that there are many, many people living in a small room or apartment. It is very unfair that in a land of so much wealth and opportunity there is so much poverty in parts of Canada. It is very unfair that in Halifax, which has a very large black population, 75 per cent of young black people are without work. Only 20 young blacks graduated from high school in 1984. There is obviously something wrong when we have a society like the one we have which is so wealthy and so rich yet we have so many people living in absolute poverty.
We also heard from women, Mr. Speaker. We heard from the Status of Women group in Newfoundland. We heard from Beth Lacy and we heard from Dorothy Engels in the City of
St. John's. They told us about discrimination in jobs when it comes to women. They told us that they estimate as a result of their work and research that around 45 per cent of the women in Newfoundland are unemployed. They also told us that in Newfoundland there are very few daycare centres for parents who want to leave their children in daycare while they go to work. They said that Newfoundland has by far the worst record in all of Canada in terms of spaces in daycare centres and in terms of the proportion of daycare centres for the population of that province. They also told us about the large number of women who want to work and cannot find full-time jobs, who are working at very low income and part-time jobs because of the tremendous recession and depression in the economy of Newfoundland.
We also spoke with a representative of disabled Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, his name was Shawn McCormick, from Halifax. He said that about 10 per cent of Canadians are disabled. This is something that I, and I think many people with me and many of my colleagues, tend to forget. He said that although the disabled represent 10 per cent of our population, federal spending for the disabled in this country has dropped in the last three or four years. He also said that although there is a great deal of unemployment among disabled Canadians, there is only one co-ordinator for the disabled in the four Atlantic provinces, only one for the province of Quebec and only one person co-ordinating programs for the disabled in Ontario, and there is only one person for the four remaining western provinces.
Mr. Speaker, it is not fair, in a country that has so much wealth and resources, to have-

-to have such a little money going to people who are disabled. That is one change we should be making. The Hon. Member for Moncton (Mr. Cochrane) says we have had a lot of task forces. My understanding, according to Mr. McCormick who appeared before us, is that they made 19 recommendations and only six of them have been acted upon by the Parliament of Canada. I suggest that it is time we got our act together collectively in terms of doing something for the disabled in Canada. We have, as was mentioned before, the recommendations of Judge Abella whose report came down in the latter part of November. She made recommendations about employment equity for disabled people. The first objective of the action group on jobs was to give ordinary Canadians a forum in which to speak out and tell us about their problems, whether they be disabled, women, fishermen, loggers, miners, young people or whoever.

Our second objective as we went across the country was to try to discover some new ideas from the people of Canada. I genuinely feel that there are no experts in this regard. I do not feel that there are any experts in terms of creating jobs. The best experts are the ordinary people of Canada. They know their communities best. They live in them. They have a better idea than most of us as to what should be done. We came across many new ideas. I suppose if there was a theme, the theme was that in the past there have been too many centralist programs imposed by Ottawa or by St. John's, Newfoundland or by Halifax, Nova Scotia. There have been too many centralist programs devised by economists, too many theories about how to put people to work or about how to organize industry. We were told time and time again that they had too many such programs.
They said that they wanted a more decentralized approach based upon the self-reliance of various communities. They wanted small-scale development based upon local economies. They wanted more decentralization, not megaprojects and large spending programs as they have seen so often in the past. In fact, Michael Kay, a representative of the Social Action Committee of the Archdiocese of St. John's, said, "What we should have are employment strategies that are based on small scale industrial approaches throughout the Province of Newfoundland". He also said, "We need more worker-producer co-ops in the Province of Newfoundland".
We heard from students Gavin Will and Nina Patey from Memorial University who said that they needed more incentives and more help for small business in Newfoundland. They said that they needed more encouragement from the federal and provincial Governments for the co-operative movement which worked so successfully in the Province of Quebec-
[ Translation]
-in the province of Quebec and in my own province of Saskatchewan, where the co-operative movement is very strong-

We have had a lot of success with it. We heard from Keith Davis from the Newfoundland Unemployment Action Committee, who said, "What we need are more community-based developments. We need local control. What we need is local initiative".
I think the message from these people is a very clear one. The direction in which we should go is helping people to help themselves. We should try to develop appropriate industries and businesses based upon local communities. We should take a serious look at trying to establish more assistance and set up co-operatives and at trying to help the co-operative movement.
Then we heard a couple of ideas about taxation which I think are interesting and at which I think we in the House should take a look. A university professor by the name of Bob Hill talked about the fact that most jobs in the country are created by small business. He made the point that we have a flat tax for corporations. Whether or not they make a large or a small profit, there is a flat tax for corporations. He suggested

taking a look at changing it from a flat tax to a progressive tax for corporations. For example, a small company which was not making much money would pay a much lower corporate rate, and a larger company making a killing would have its tax rate rising very progressively in a similar way as now applies to individuals in Canada. I think that is an idea worth looking at. Perhaps it might be one way to help small businesses in Canada. It also might be a way of raising revenue from the large and wealthy corporations which are doing very well. He also said that we should take a look at special taxes when it comes to single-industry towns and communities. Often a big company will come into a community because the market internationally is very good. It makes a lot of money, a large profit, and then the market turns down, the mine closes, the company disappears and everyone is laid off. He suggested that we should look at the possibility of a special levy or a special tax when times are good placed on big companies in single-industry towns. He suggested that that tax should be turned over, not to the federal Government or the provincial Government for its plans and ideas, but to the local municipality, town, village or whatever in order to diversify the economy or the economic base of the particular community.
If such legislation had been in effect years ago, perhaps Schefferville would still exist as a fairly decent community within which to live, with a few opportunities for its people despite the fact that Iron Ore closed down that particular mine.
These were some of the ideas of ordinary people who appeared before the task force. After the first few days of setting up this action group on jobs. I knew there were many people out there who had many ideas. They have stories to tell about what we can do in their communities. The general theme was to look at appropriate, small-scale development, particularly in places like Newfoundland and Cape Breton where there are many small communities-perhaps a job here, five jobs there and ten jobs there, but jobs which will be permanent, long-term and relevant to their particular economies.
As I said, there were three objectives. The first was to give people a forum and the second was to get some new ideas. The third objective was to try, through this mechanism and others, to ensure that the job issue remained as the number one issue on the parliamentary agenda and to ensure that it was the most important issue addressed by the Government and indeed by all parliamentarians in the House of Commons. If we could use this mechanism to give people a forum in which to present new ideas and to put pressure upon us as Members of Parliament so that we deal with the issue, I think we are making a great contribution to the future of the country.
I feel very positive about our opportunities in Canada. I feel we can put the unemployed to work. I feel we can put young people to work. We can become a nation of producers. We can own and control our own economy. We can do all those things, but we will only do it if this House of

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) for bringing this motion before the House today. I feel it is a very important and urgent question. I congratulate him for taking the initiative to bring this as an NDP opposition motion. I would particularly like to say how much I agree with his opening statement. He said that the House should recognize the extreme urgency of the unemployment crisis in Atlantic Canada. The Hon. Member toured Atlantic Canada for three days with other members of his Party. I also congratulate him for the initiative he took in that regard. I do not downplay the fact that he did not spend a longer period of time there. I realize the time constraints which he has as a Member of Parliament which did not make it possible for him to spend a great deal of time there.
As a Member of Parliament from that region I would like to say that what he saw and heard is only a small part of the depth and concern that exists in that part of Canada. We have all spoken in the House about how marginal are the pensions for senior citizens. I can tell Members of the House that I constantly meet with constituents who are living with three or four of their brothers or sisters or offspring as well as their parents. Three generations are living together. The income which is keeping that family alive is the pension or pensions of the grandparents or parents. That is the only income in that family, and that is not an exception. It is a very serious situation.
Although I do not disagree with the four points which the Hon. Member makes, I would not want the House to believe that these four points will put us well on the way to correcting the unemployment situation and the problem of regional disparity in our area, because they will not. As accurate as they are, they do not go nearly far enough to correct the situation. He says that we need proper resource management to rebuild

He says that we need self-directed community programs to expand permanent jobs through co-operatives and small business. This is very important. The greatest problem of small businesses is where to get capital. Who will invest in a business in a depressed area of high unemployment and regional disparity? Yet the Government is practically encouraging the Federal Business Development Bank to be a profitable corporation. Is that agency there to help areas of high unemployment with regional disparity, or is it there to make a profit? The Government must decide that.
In Sydney, Nova Scotia, whether or not you give a personal guarantee, you cannot get a commercial mortgage from a bank or a finance company. How can you have small business if the normal channels of commerce will not help you? The Government says that it can be done through the private sector. Mr. Speaker, the private sector has been tried and found wanting. What is going to be done?
The problem begins with the Government. You have only to look at the economic and fiscal statement to see which area of Canada was most affected. The Government has said that the Atlantic region is expendable in the next election if it cannot please all areas. You do not need it written out for you; you need only read the economic and fiscal statement.
Look at the attitude of the Minister. Members in his Party cannot tell me that the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) is sympathetic to regional development. No one who has spoken to the Minister will have heard any indication that this is a concern of his. I am not saying this to be critical. I wish he were in the House now so that I could tell him this. The Minister is from Toronto and he may not have a feeling for it. I honestly hope that I am wrong or that he can develop that feeling for it. However, at the present time I sincerely do not think he has a feeling for regional development.
This is a serious matter because, as the Minister said this morning, he is also chairman of the caucus committee on economic and regional development in the Government. That is a tremendously important position. As he said, he co-ordinates all the Departments. Regional development is the coordination of the activity, finance and input of all Departments. Regional development is made up of transportation, trade and commerce, training and grants. It is all-encompassing. There is a total lack of understanding in this very important area.
The Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) asked what the Liberal Government had done. I agree that the Liberal Government has not provided all the answers. In fact, I still say that one of the worst mistakes it made was to disband DREE. I agree completely. The reason disbanding DREE was such a mistake is not the obvious one. It is because we brought
DREE and Industry, Trade and Commerce together. The people in IT and C, who are not at all concerned with regional development, were able to overshadow and smother the voices of reason which existed within DREE. The thinking of IT and C completely took over and smothered the concept of regional development.
When this Government came to power there was one little problem which remained. In the areas of Canada where regional development was a major question and IT and C and DREE had joined, DREE was a larger agency, so its thinking was able to predominate. The Minister ignored them completely. If you went to the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion now and asked a question, they would not answer, as was the case with the previous Liberal Government. They would not say that they were not allowed to comment because it had not been approved or passed. The Department will not tell you that. People there will say, "We don't know. We do not know what is going on. We are not involved in this". What you have, Mr. Speaker, in areas in this country are trained professionals in regional expansion and regional development who have absolutely no input into areas for which they are supposed to be responsible.
Let me come to the recent announcement about Pratt and Whitney, on which I congratulate the Government. It is an excellent decision and it will be good for Nova Scotia. I have one concern. I could not find out in Halifax, in Moncton, the regional office, nor in Ottawa what the federal input was. Nobody knew. I know that the Province of Nova Scotia is not going to finance the whole amount. I do not care whether the money comes from the federal Government or the provincial Government. Don't get me wrong, Mr. Speaker. My concern, and I said this to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), is the precedent that Members of Parliament, people and concerned individuals will not be able to find out exactly what is transpiring in the Province of Nova Scotia, in other provinces and in regions of this country in which they have a vested interest. My goodness, people who live in areas of regional disparity have more of a vested interest in their area than people in economically successful areas. They have been deprived. They lack things that people in other areas take for granted. They really have paid the price to be able to know what is going on.
I say again to the Minister of Defence (Mr. Coates) that the same thing is now going on with regard to the Sydney Steel Corporation. There is no written formal request from the Province of Nova Scotia to the federal Government requesting funding for the second phase of the Sydney Steel Corporation. There is no question about that. I know that the Minister, the Solicitor General (Mr. MacKay), the Premier and the Minister for Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) have had meetings. But there has been no formal request from the province, yet this is a provincial Crown corporation. Is it not reasonable to expect the Province of Nova Scotia to write formally to the federal Government and tell the federal Government what it wants? What is going on here? What kind of a shell game is this where the whole thing is shuffled, money

will be doled out, but no one will know on what basis? No one will know the business plan used for the first stage or the funding on which the first phase was based. Was it based on the business plan that we requested? We wanted to make sure that the funding was going to be used in the interests and for the success of the industry and ultimately the success of the region. If we do not know on what it was based, we will not know whether it was applied properly. This is improper. This is not only bad government, but it is completely betraying the trust of the people whom this Government says it wants to benefit. This is incredible, Mr. Speaker.
This Government has said that Devco, the Cape Breton Development Corporation, had losses. Sure Devco had losses. But what has the Government done? It has gone to the other extreme completely. There is no knowledge of what is going on. The Minister says he is going to make important announcements, but nobody knows what those announcements are going to be. No one knows on what basis they are going to be made. The corporation has completely strangled all activity. It has two divisions, a coal division and an industrial development division. Nothing is being allowed to go on. At the first of last year a firm of consultants did a study as to what changes should be made in the corporation. The draft of that study was ready in August, but it has still not been released. People wonder where their jobs are. They cannot operate efficiently under a situation like that. It is very serious.
The Minister said this morning that money was just put away and thrown out. Every time people from Atlantic Canada say they are not getting anything, they are told they are making a political football of the area. There are people with no incomes other than pensions. Families consisting of four and five people are living on that. I am supposed to be afraid to comment on that because I would be making a political football out of it. What kind of callousness and inconsideration is that?
The Minister gave a speech this morning. It was uninformative and condescending. It just made a joke out of this very important question. It is not a joke. It is an extremely serious situation. I do not have to limit these comments to Altantic Canada. This Government is blind to a very real problem in the country. What is developing in this country is not only developing in Altantic Canada but, unfortunately, this is the only sector on which we have taken the lead.
In Toronto you see hopelessness. People have no hope for the future in this technological age. There is no way of being retrained. The Government does not want to retrain them. The most precious thing in this country is the life of each individual. This Government says that there is no hope for fulfillment or a chance to live this life to the fullest. What is developing? I cannot overemphasize that what is developing is a society within a society. The society we see officially is the upwardly mobile society with education and aspirations. What the Government wants to suppress is the society without hope, without jobs and incomes. But they want to be able to eat and live and to have things even in a small way that ordinary Canadians take for granted. I see people like that in my constituency. I

see them all the time; included are young people who went to school and finished school. Many of them have one or two college degrees but they have nothing to look forward to. Yet when the jobs become available there will be a group who will graduate behind them and you will hear, "These students and young people have been unemployed for three years. Obviously they do not want to work". This is callousness of the highest order. It just will not wash.
The Government says it wants to develop regional development. But it does not know what regional development means. The Government says, and the Minister of National Defence can substantiate that, it that has allocated $8 million for the City of Sydney in a subsidiary agreement with the Province of Nova Scotia, which the province did not go into. That $8 million was passed by the Cabinet of the former Liberal Government and passed by Treasury Board. The subsidiary agreement was brought up, but where is the $8 million? If the Government is so concerned with regional disparity, why does it not at least put money that has been passed to work?
What about the income security office that was cancelled as a result of the economic and fiscal statement on November 8? This office was supposed to decentralize 85 jobs from Halifax to Sydney. The federal Government had already spent $1 million on decentralization. People had been trained. Perhaps they had opportunities for other jobs. Others had given up jobs in the hope they could have one of the positions in Sydney. But the Government cancelled the decentralization. Where did the $1 million go? This was a $2.1 million saving. One million dollars was wasted, of which $400,000 was to renovate a building that still stands unoccupied. This was an industry with a potential for employment. It had a potential for spinoffs that could develop with immunity and provide economic stimulation for an area that badly needed it.
If we are going to create regional development we have to do something with the communities. What if an oil company says it wants to locate in a certain place? Is the Government going to say that because it is going to give the company such and such a percentage of financing the company has to go to such and such a place? The oil company people will laugh. The oil company will go where it wants to. The oil industry and any industry will say to the Government, "We will go there, or we will go somewhere else, or we will not go at all". If Pratt and Whitney had said, "We are going to Halifax and that is it," what would the Government have said? Would the Government have said, "No, Pratt and Whitney, you are going somewhere else"? It is not that Pratt and Whitney would have said that, I am just using Pratt and Whitney as an example. This is a serious situation. It is not a situation that can be dealt with in simplicity. It takes work, but it also takes compassion and interest toward the people affected.
