the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) who introduced the motion today. 1 was not a member of the task force which visited Atlantic Canada on behalf of the New Democratic Party. However, I have travelled there in the past as the co-ordinator of Atlantic issues in our caucus. As a result, I have had an opportunity to visit many of the communities visited by the task force over the last little while as well as some other communities. I am glad to see the Hon. Member for Annapoplis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) present in the House for the short time he has been with us today. I congratulate him upon having an NDP MLA elected in his riding. That will be of long-term benefit to the people of that riding.
Seriously speaking, the people of the Atlantic region have some very peculiar and special problems which have not been addressed by government over the last many years. Certainly Governments, both Conservatives and Liberal, both provincial and federal, have thrown money at various problems. Money has been thrown at Sysco. Money has been spent on Devco. Money has been spent on the fishing industry and on the forest industry. Money has been spent to keep this plant and that plant going. However, there has never been any concrete economic planning done with the people of the regions.
In travelling through that region I learned that basically governments do not listen to the people of the region. In the briefs which our force received over the last week in Atlantic Canada there were a number of different ideas presented by co-ops, unions, social action committees, community development associations and others concerned about what was happening in their community. I discovered that time after time local people were not listened to and that the people who worked in Sysco and in Devco were not listened to. For example, the people working in Sysco can tell us that the coke oven is falling apart or that some things have not been rehabilitated for 30 years or 40 years. They can tell us where the bottlenecks in the plant are. However, when decisions are made, they tend to be made by government officials or by company officials who have really not taken the time to understand the problems of the plant. Quite often that is more true when a government is running the operation. The reason I say this, although I am a socialist, is that because governments running operations, whether they be at Sysco or Devco, do not really believe that they can do a good job at managing the operations. It is not a priority of the Government of Nova Scotia to ensure that Sysco is doing well. It was not a priority of the previous federal Liberal Government to ensure that Devco was running well. That is the problem. If we do not have a commitment to make something work it will not work.
I listened to the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys (Mr. MacLellan) talk about how sad he was to see that the Department of Regional Economic Expansion was closed down and became incorporated as part of the new DRIE. He explained that obviously the people in Regional Economic Expansion lost influence, that they had less to do with actual decision making within the new Department and that the people running the new Department, including the Minister,
were really not listening to the people in charge of Regional Economic Expansion. That is something which I said as former spokesman for the NDP caucus on regional economic expansion. I said that we needed a separate organization within government concerned about regional economic expansion out there working with the people and the companies to ensure that economic expansion was taking place within the regions. Unfortunately, Industry, Trade and Commerce has different priorities. In its plannings it reacts and acts upon its own priorities.
I believe that things can be done for Atlantic Canada. As was indicated in the motion, we can build our industries upon the resources of forestry, fishing and coal. We can listen to the people and work through community programs. We can have affirmative action to help women in high unemployment regions of the country. We can develop the steel industry through Crown corporations. However, we can only do that if the people in planning in government listen to the people affected and make the development of Crown corporations, community-based programs and businesses a strong priority.
The problem in part faced by Devco, Sysco and the fishing industry has been the lack of a real commitment by government or by the senior bureaucrats who advise government. The responsibility cannot rest only with senior advisers to government. Responsibility in a parliamentary democracy must rest with Cabinet Ministers. They are the ones who must ensure that their own advisers are working full out and giving direction to their own workforces to ensure, for example, that a roof at Sysco is not caving in. When I visited the Sysco operation three years ago, that was literally the case. As we walked through its plant we noticed that parts of the roof were slowly falling to the ground. That had been the case for years, and nothing was done about it. It was the same at Devco. More development had to take place there. No one was doing anything about it. The Cabinet Ministers of the Liberal Government at that time were not making anything happen. They were not ensuring that Departments were active or that the Cape Breton Development Corporation was developing the mine to its best capabilities.
I realize I do not have much time to speak on this motion. However, I should like to point out that when we listen to the people, we hear suggestions and ideas which will make a big difference. In the brief submitted to the task force by local 1064 of the United Steelworkers of America in Cape Breton, there were a number of suggestions about the development of Sydney Steel. They talked about the need to finish products in that operation. They pointed out that in the history of the Sysco operation at one time it was part of an integrated system for the development and finishing of steel. However, when Hawker Siddeley pulled out of Cape Breton, it left only part of an operation which was not integrated with the other aspects of the steel industry. Right from the beginning we had a Crown corporation which did not meet the needs of a modern integrated steel industry. Ever since that time, even though a lot of money was poured into Sydney Steel, there was never a

development plan which would produce the finished products that Sydney Steel needed.
I do not have time to read it all, but it is interesting to read how the steel workers presented a number of suggestions in terms of developing wire rod products, light structural steel, by-products from coke. They went through the different means of modernizing the Sydney Steel plant which is so important to the community.
It was interesting listening to the spokesmen from the co-operative movements. The Cape Breton Co-Operative Council made a presentation to the task force. M. N. Cote, a great leader of the co-operative movement, was quoted. He talked about the necessity of having an attitude whereby we and others who are concerned can develop our ideas not just about profits and dividends, but about developing our community and having a different feeling about what it means to be in business. To be in business is not just to take money from the community. It must be a part of your whole self. You are part of the community, part of the greater world.
What was the basis of the strength of the co-operative movement in Cape Breton? That ideal is something that Government must consider more. It must consider the development of community businesses. They are not there just to make the dollar. There is nothing wrong with making a dollar. Obviously people are in business for a purpose, the same as people take a job for a purpose, but there has to be more to it than that.
A major problem is that federal and provincial Governments tend to look at the megaprojects. When I was spokesman for regional economic expansion, one year I received figures on what was happening with some DREE programs. It was interesting to note that when you broke down the money for industrial incentives, in one particular year $75 million went to what were considered large corporations. They produced 4,691 jobs. That same year, $25 million in federal government money went to small corporations and small operations, and they produced 4,681 jobs. The Government gave the large corporations an extra $50 million, three times as much as it gave to the small corporations, and they produced only 10 more jobs. It will be interesting to know how many of those large operations are in business today and producing the products which the federal Government paid to be produced.
That proves the bias that exists in too many government programs. The money is given to the large operators but they do not necessarily produce that many jobs. Many small manufacturing companies and industries produce long-term jobs in a particular community. The whole approach of Government in underdeveloped areas, such as Atlantic Canada with a number of small and medium sized communities with high unemployment rates, should be to look at the small fish plants, small lightbulk factories and other small operations which remain in a community and produce jobs for people in that area. It is important that the woodlot owners be considered in any forest

industry program. That is something that the Government obviously is not doing.
I recognize that my time is almost up and that others wish to speak, so I will conclude with a few short words. I hope that in the next little while this House again develops the ability to look at expansion on a regional basis. The debate today, which basically focused on Atlantic Canada, has given us that opportunity. It was nice to hear a Liberal back-bencher who was previously the Parliament Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-The Sydneys, admit that a mistake was made. I hope the new Government will bring back the Department of Regional Economic Expansion so that there is a Department specifically working for development of the regions and sub-regions of this country. This is important and necessary. Under DRIE or the other Departments, the underdeveloped regions of this country will never be developed. The people in those regions will not be listened to and they will not know who is making the decisions that affect their lives.

I would suggest that the Party across the aisle might ask the Leader of the New Democratic Party in Nova Scotia to welcome this type of investment. I certainly welcome it. I do not believe that the people of Nova Scotia are against the creation of a thousand new jobs.
Before resuming my seat, I would like to comment on the suggestion of the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond that the private sector cannot take up the slack of creating jobs. I shall quote from a recent article in The Globe and Mail which reads as follows:
But few businessmen are complaining about the Conservative Government so far.
"A lot of the responsibility now will rely on people like ourselves who are running companies and employing people to generate work,"-
This was said by Mr. Rowe, the President of both IMP Group Ltd. of Halifax and the Halifax Board of Trade. He went on to say:
"Jobs may come particularly in the export fields, but it's up to the private sector to create those jobs ... working closely with government."
I would like to relate a little conversation I had with a businessman from Halifax while on the airplane from Nova Scotia last week. This businessman said: "Thank God, Mr. Comeau, that you form the Government. We were starting to lose hope and confidence, and it was about time you people went in and started doing the kind of confidence building that you have been doing over the past few months. Keep up the good work, and if you want any further comments like this one, I will be glad to get many more business people to pass these kinds of comments on".
In closing, I would invite the Hon. Member for Essex-Wind-sor to return to Atlantic Canada at any time in order to see what is happening down there. I think he will find that there are a lot of people with optimism who are happy about the way things are going. In echoing some of the comments made by the Hon. Member from Moncton earlier this afternoon, I would say, let us not create patchwork programs. Let us get on and rebuild all of the regions of Canada. Let us rebuild not only Atlantic Canada but Quebec, central Canada and the West as well. Let us bring it all in under one truly national Party.

speechtext: Questions or comments? Resuming debate.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to take up this debate from the point at which it was left by the Hon. Member for South West Nova (Mr. Comeau). I certainly appreciate his contribution to the debate. As he was concluding he said that he had been speaking with some business people from the Atlantic Provinces who said that they were beginning to lose hope and confidence and that that was why they were happy to see a change in government. While I was happy to see a change in government, I think that the Hon. Member for South West Nova and members of his Party should realize that there are a lot of unemployed Canadians in Atlantic Canada and across the country who have been losing hope and confidence because of the situation they face. They cannot see light at the end of the tunnel. They recognize now that it may be a fact that a recovery which does the private sector good may not in fact be a recovery that puts them back to work.
There have been two years of economic recovery in this country and yet the unemployment rate is still approaching 11 per cent. That is a modest improvement from a few months ago; nonetheless, it is a level of unemployment which would have been intolerable just a few short years ago.
When our task force on jobs went to Atlantic Canada, met with people and began to look at alternative policies, it began to recognize that Atlantic Canada has some particular problems caused by its dependence on resource-based industries and the fact that most parts of Atlantic Canada are distant from the major markets of Canada which are in Montreal, the Provinces of Quebec and Ontario and the West. Therefore, it faces heavy transportation costs and difficulties in terms of access to other parts of the domestic market here in Canada.
Atlantic Canada faces real problems, and one of the problems is that the private sector has shown a willingness to overlook Atlantic Canada in a pretty consistent fashion over the course of the last few years. Where the private sector has been prepared to come into Atlantic Canada, the conditions that multinational enterprises have set have been conditions that I for one and my Party in general find very difficult to tolerate.
I can recall, for example, the anti-labour bias of the Miche-lin Corporation which led to its having the Nova Scotia Government pass specific legislation that effectively gutted the
January 25, 1985

labour laws of that province at a time when the workers of the two tire plants run by Michelin were on the verge of getting certification for their trade union. I can recall similarly the Newfoundland Government snapping to attention when it was asked to implement anti-labour legislation in connection with the pulp and paper mill in Corner Brook in the very recent past.
That kind of behaviour is what leads people in my Party to feel that a reliance on the private sector alone will not be enough to bring Atlantic Canadians back to a level of employment, prosperity and hope for the future that we believe they deserve. That is why we began this task force on jobs by going to Atlantic Canada, and why we will now continue looking at some of the same issues in other parts of the country in addition to returning to Atlantic Canada later on in the tour.
I recall that during the election campaign, members of the Progressive Conservative Party said that their platform was jobs, jobs, jobs. We found out on November 8 that that priority had changed and that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had decided that the priority was to overcome the deficit and, once the deficit had been overcome, then perhaps enough confidence would be reinstated in the private sector to somehow begin to create a resurgence of economic activity in the country.
My colleagues from British Columbia can tell the House that the resurgence of confidence in the business sector, if it has occurred, has certainly not had an impact on that province. If anything, the situation in that province is worse than it was just a few short months ago. There has not been a resurgence there and that province has had the dubious benefit of two and a half years of cuts and reductions in government spending and of the other kinds of nostrums or remedies which the Minister of Finance wishes to impose upon the country as a whole. If those remedies are imposed on the country as a whole, then I regret to say that we may see the consequences in Atlantic Canada which we are now seeing in British Columbia of a further increase in unemployment and less confidence and hope for the future than that which exists today.
My colleagues on the task force who visited Atlantic Canada, as was faithfully and warmly mirrored in the speeches made by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor and the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), found that despite all the adversity and problems, there is still a great deal of courage and hope for the future among the ordinary Canadians who came individually and in groups to speak to the task force in Nova Scotia and in Newfoundland. They found that people were prepared to seize opportunities but that they were looking for partnership, for open doors and for ways that they could rebuild and re-base the economy of Atlantic Canada using new techniques and alternatives.
One of the reasons why we have the task force to which the New Democratic Party has committed so many resources is our sense that it is time for all of us in this country and all of us in this Parliament from whatever Party not to look back in
Supply
the past to the days of Adam Smith, as the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) seems to want to do. We should not be looking backwards to what happened in 1979 or 1980, as so many of the Conservatives seem to want to do when they rise and talk about our Party. We should not be looking backwards to some golden age of capitalism and free enterprise, but we should be looking forward with an appreciation of the economic problems and opportunities which we in this country face over the course of the next decade or two. I believe we must do this with a sense of urgency. That urgency is certainly reflected in the wording of the motion which was put forward by the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon). The fact is that 13 per cent or 14 per cent of the population of Atlantic Canada is unemployed now, and there are many more people in Atlantic Canada who have become so discouraged that they are not looking for a job at all. Among young people in Newfoundland the unemployment rate exceeds 20 per cent, and all that the Conservatives in Newfoundland can offer their Government is the fact that after six years in power a royal commission has been set up to see whether there are solutions which could be found. That is an answer, Mr. Speaker, which I certainly believe is totally inadequate.
When I say we must start to look for alternative solutions, I think, among other things, that this House and the Government of Canada should be aware of the kind of ferment which is taking place around us, both in Canada and in other countries around the world. I was struck when I was in England two years ago at the birth and growth of the co-operative enterprise there which has been created by trades people, young workers and other people because of the economic disaster which has been brought on by the Government of Margaret Thatcher. There are new kinds of enterprises which are growing there, Mr. Speaker, not to overcome the problems but at least as a response to the problems. Despite the adversity of the economic climate in Britain, some new things are happening in that country.
I was struck when I was in Minneapolis about three years ago that in that State there was a far more diverse range of different responses to economic problems than I had expected to find in my preconceived notion. There were all kinds of mixed enterprises and joint task forces and so on providing community services and community economic development. We have seen that in this country as well, Mr. Speaker. We have seen the growth of alternative industries and the birth and creation of new ways of doing work and organizing enterprises in the private sector, the co-operative sector and through joint operations in which perhaps provincial Governments, perhaps municipal Governments and private individuals have become involved. Those kinds of alternatives, it seems to be, should be encouraged and not discouraged.
That is one of the reasons I am disappointed in some of the early signs of a new Government which promised change when it came to power on September 4. The signs are that this Government does not appear to understand that at all. Just around Christmas, the Minister responsible for housing, his

January 25, 1985
Supply
Department and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation took away 500 units of grants from co-operative and non-profit housing corporations and gave them to developers in the private sector. Perhaps that could be seen as a small step, Mr. Speaker, but it was a brutal blow to an important part of the housing industry and a part of the housing industry which I believe ought to be allowed to grow and not to die. One of the consequences of the November 8 cuts was that there was a cut of $16 million on an annual basis in the federal Government's program through the National Research Council of support for research and development in the alternative energy industries, including solar, wind, peat, hydrogen and conservation energy, a whole range of technologies which were being developed by a rapidly growing and very important new industry. This is an industry which I believe should be particularly important to Atlantic Canada because of its dependence right now on petroleum based energy. The fact is that until today there has not been the success we all had hoped to see in terms of actually delivering the petroleum and natural gas resources which appear to lie offshore in Atlantic Canada. Even when those petroleum resources are developed, Mr. Speaker, there will be important markets for them in the United States and in the rest of Canada. Conservation and alternative energies form an opportunity for new industries in the private sector in Atlantic Canada and for ways in which Atlantic Canada can overcome its chronic and long-standing energy deficits.
This resolution speaks about a revitalization of the coal industry in Cape Breton, which is another way of overcoming the region's energy related deficit. What is happening, Mr. Speaker, in that particular area, is that the National Research Council's division of energy has pulled the rug out from under a lot of the companies which were pioneering in this particular area just at a time when those technologies were becoming competitive with traditional forms of energy. I cite that as example because it seems to me that the new Government should be encouraging alternatives, new ideas and new approaches to doing things. That is what we are trying to do through the means of our task force. One of the things that we can do as an opposition Party is to go out and listen to Canadians.
The Hon. Member for Moncton (Mr. Cochrane), I believe, started to attack this Party for having a task force at all, apparently having forgotten the degree to which those task forces were used by his Party when those Hon. Members were sitting on this side of the House of Commons. I make no apology for this approach at all. It seems to me that that is one of the vital functions which we in an opposition Party can perform. But we need to do more than to listen to Canadians. We need action as well. That is why our task force is going to devote itself to finding plans for action and alternatives which can be practically implemented in order to ensure that jobs will be created for the people of Atlantic Canada and for the people in the rest of Canada as well.
One of the criticisms which is beginning to emerge of the desire for consultation on the part of the new Government is the fact that it seems to want to listen forever but does not do
anything. It seems to have forgotten about the need to produce some of its plans in the form of white papers which would result in a more constructive form of consultation. There are some very serious problems there, Mr. Speaker, in terms of the fact that the Government does not understand that when one consults, one has to be committed to action as well, and that action is not forthcoming.

Mr. Speaker, in listening to his comments, I noticed that the Hon. Member for Moncton (Mr. Cochrane) said the proposals made by the New Democratic Party were not far-reaching enough to respond to the economic crisis in the Atlantic provinces. I agree that the motion presented by the Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon) could have been a bit longer and more detailed, but nevertheless, we tried to concentrate on the most important factors that would at least start the process of rebuilding the economy in the Atlantic provinces.
We, on our side, Mr. Speaker, are engaged in a participatory process consisting of discussions and meetings with people from the Maritimes and also from Quebec, Ontario and the Western provinces.
At this point, I would like to say a few words about the situation in the province of Quebec. I noticed that in his speech, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) made no reference to the situation in the St. Maurice area which is now suffering the effects of shutdowns at the Wabasso and Melchers plants.
Here we have an example of problems created by the private sector for which the private sector has no solution. A comprehensive policy requires a commitment on the part of the Government, not just speeches in praise of the private sector. It requires specific practical measures, measures that must relate to the skills of people, of small businesses and businessmen in the regions, if they are to create jobs.
Up to now, Mr. Speaker, we have seen that this Government has tended to go on about the importance of the private sector, while ignoring the problems facing Canadians in all regions of this country, a country where we unfortunately still have an unemployment rate of over 11 per cent, and now 12 per cent in the province of Quebec.

I want to conclude, Mr. Speaker, by saying that I am proud of the work our task force on jobs is doing. I intend to be with the task force when we visit Quebec, Chicoutimi, and the Lac Saint Jean area in the course of the next week or so. I hope and believe very strongly that we will have constructive alternatives to put forward over the life of this task force which will have real meaning to the people of Canada and which we expect to see acted upon by the Government if it is really

committed to the change it promised during the election campaign.
